# Concept types

To the better understanding, we grouped those highly relevant entities to six concepts types as shown below:
(1) Gene: it includes genes, proteins, mRNA and other gene products.
(2) Chemical: it contents chemical and drug.
(3) Disease : it contents diseases, symptoms, and some disease-related phenotypes.
(4) Variant : it contents the genomic/protein variants (including substitutions, deletions, insertions, and others).
(5) Species: it includes the species in the hierarchical taxonomy of organisms.
(6) CellLine: cell line.

# Guideline of the entities

## General rules

- Annotate all the spans of all the six concept types.
- The full text can be accessed to clarify the concept spans and identifiers.
- The abbreviation and its long form should be annotated separately if possible. prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) in the text, “prostaglandin E2” and “PGE2” should be both annotated to chemicals with the same identifier (D015232).
- Annotate both the full name and abbreviation in one entity, if the boundary of the entity covers both of them. For instance, annotate “Deoxyguanosine kinase (dGK) deficiency” entirely to a disease (PMID:19394258).
- Annotate the composite entity spans (e.g., “MMP-1, -2”) entirely.
- Annotate the concept spans with misspelling (“HLRRC” in PMID:18366737).

## Gene

- Annotate the gene families including paralogs/orthologs (e.g., bone morphogenetic protein(bmp)), but DO NOT annotate the functional based families (e.g., tumor suppressor gene, protein kinase).
- Following the previous rule, if at least one of the gene family members mentioned in the text, the identifiers of those members are assigned to the family name (e.g., in “Cytochrome P-450 genes (CYP1A1, CYP2A6, CYP2D6, and CYP2E1)”, Cytochrome P-450 genes should be assigned with NCBI Gene: 1543,1548,1565,1571). If no family member is in the text, the first gene reached in the gene family should be assigned (e.g., matrix metalloproteinases to NCBI Gene:4312(MMP1)).
- In experimental studies, annotate the gene identifier corresponding to the organism/species that is the source of the gene (for example mouse gene transfected into human cells is annotated to record for mouse gene).
- DO NOT annotate the genes, if they are named for cells and pathways.

## Disease

- Annotate the diseased-related phenotypes but not other (e.g., short ear in PMID:17345627).
- DO NOT annotate the high-level diseases (e.g., “genetic disorder”).
  Excludes:
  - Cis-acting disease (PMID:12442272)
  - genetic disorders (PMID:18046082)
  - familial disorder (PMID:20806042)
- Annotate “drug addiction” to “disease”.
- Annotate the symptoms to diseases.
- DO NOT annotate overdose.
- DO NOT annotate the mental status and phenotypes to diseases unless the term is exactly recorded in MEDIC. e.g., decline in sympathetic tone (PMID:19067809)
- DO NOT annotate references to biological processes such as “tumorigenesis” or “cancerogenesis”.
- Annotate minimum necessary text spans for a disease. For example, select “hypertension” instead of “sustained hypertension.”, unless the span covers the prefix or the suffix can exactly match a specific concept identifier (e.g., “chronic bronchitis” to D029481).

## Chemical

- Annotate the chemical abbreviation with the dose. For example “In addition, GABA content of mice hippocampus treated with GFC75 plus P400 showed an increase of 46.90% when compared with seized mice.”, 75 and 400 suffixes are the doses. In this case, we annotate GFC75 and P400 as chemical spans. (PMID:24911645).
- Annotate the chemical resource for extracts, e.g., “ethanolic extract of Daucus carota seeds (DCE)” in PMID:16755009; “grape seed proanthocyanidin extract” in PMID:11334364.
- DO NOT annotate antibodies to chemicals. (PMID:17595233) (PMID:20648600)
- DO NOT annotate saline, placebo, water, and juice.
- DO NOT annotate residue, free radicals.
- DO NOT annotate staining chemical (e.g., hematoxylin in PMID:24442316)
- DO NOT annotate vaccines.

## Species

- DO NOT annotate beyond species rank (e.g., annotate homo sapiens but do not annotate mammalian which is a taxonomy class)

## Variant

- DO NOT annotate residue of the gene modification.

## Conflict cases among different concept types

- [Gene/Disease] If the disease and gene share the same name, e.g., adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD) gene, annotate the concept following the below cases:
  - Adrenoleukodystrophy gene > GeneOrGeneProduct
  - Adrenoleukodystrophy patient > DiseaseOrPhenotypicFeature
  - ALD gene > GeneOrGeneProduct
  - ALD patient > DiseaseOrPhenotypicFeature
  - adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD) gene > GeneOrGeneProduct
  - adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD) patient > DiseaseOrPhenotypicFeature
- Annotate the concept with longer spans. For instance, Deoxyguanosine kinase (dGK) deficiency (MESH:C580039) instead Deoxyguanosine kinase (in PMID:19394258).
- Annotate the prefix of the corresponding species to the gene span separately (e.g., “human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-DRB1” to “human” to species and “leukocyte antigen (HLA)-DRB1” to gene).
- Annotate the virus spans (e.g., HIV-1 and HBV) to species. But annotate the infection of the virus to disease (e.g., “HIV-1 infected” maps to MESH: D015658).
- Some of the proteins can be chemicals for particular usage or purpose. We annotate the organic compounds to proteins. While, we annotate the proteins or molecules as the biologic medical products to treat diseases .
- Annotate the alleles to variants rather than chemicals, DO NOT annotate the amino acids to chemicals.
- The rule for antagonist/agonist/blocker/inhibitor: If the sentence mentions a drug/chemical and then tells the target gene, we annotate both the chemical and the gene.
- Following the previous rule, we annotate the mention to a gene if the inhibitor/blockage/agonist is part of the gene name.
  - e.g., “plasminogen activator inhibitor-1” in PMID:16167916
- Following the previous rule, if “<gene> inhibitors/agonists” is mentioned in the context of a family of compounds, without mentioning a specific drug, We annotate the entire mention (“<gene> inhibitors/agonists”) as a chemical.
  - “Methadone dose, presence of cytochrome P-450 3A4 inhibitors” in PMID:16801510
- We don’t annotate functions of genes that are described as inhibitors or activators of processes.
  - We don’t annotate “coagulation inhibitors” in PMID:17003923

## Others

- Annotate spans with morphological variations such as adjectives. For instance, annotate “hypertensive” to “hypertension”, “psychiatric” to “Mental Disorders” and “VLCAD-deficient” to “VLCAD-deficiency”.
- The suffixes of the gene/protein (e.g., “kinase” of “dGK kinase”, “gene” of “ESR1 gene”) are ignored unless the meaning is changed without the suffix (e.g., “gene” in “Becker muscular dystrophy gene”).
- DO NOT annotate the general terms such as: disease, syndrome, deficiency, complications, gene, drug, protein, nucleotide, etc. However, the disease terms such as pain, cancer, tumor, and death should be retained.

# Concept types

To the better understanding, we grouped those highly relevant entities to six concepts types as shown below:
(1) Gene: it includes genes, proteins, mRNA and other gene products.
(2) Chemical: it contents chemical and drug.
(3) Disease : it contents diseases, symptoms, and some disease-related phenotypes.
(4) Variant : it contents the genomic/protein variants (including substitutions, deletions, insertions, and others).
(5) Species: it includes the species in the hierarchical taxonomy of organisms.
(6) CellLine: cell line.

# Guideline of the entities

## General rules

- Annotate all the spans of all the six concept types.
- The full text can be accessed to clarify the concept spans and identifiers.
- The abbreviation and its long form should be annotated separately if possible. prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) in the text, “prostaglandin E2” and “PGE2” should be both annotated to chemicals with the same identifier (D015232).
- Annotate both the full name and abbreviation in one entity, if the boundary of the entity covers both of them. For instance, annotate “Deoxyguanosine kinase (dGK) deficiency” entirely to a disease (PMID:19394258).
- Annotate the composite entity spans (e.g., “MMP-1, -2”) entirely.
- Annotate the concept spans with misspelling (“HLRRC” in PMID:18366737).

## Gene

- Annotate the gene families including paralogs/orthologs (e.g., bone morphogenetic protein(bmp)), but DO NOT annotate the functional based families (e.g., tumor suppressor gene, protein kinase).
- Following the previous rule, if at least one of the gene family members mentioned in the text, the identifiers of those members are assigned to the family name (e.g., in “Cytochrome P-450 genes (CYP1A1, CYP2A6, CYP2D6, and CYP2E1)”, Cytochrome P-450 genes should be assigned with NCBI Gene: 1543,1548,1565,1571). If no family member is in the text, the first gene reached in the gene family should be assigned (e.g., matrix metalloproteinases to NCBI Gene:4312(MMP1)).
- In experimental studies, annotate the gene identifier corresponding to the organism/species that is the source of the gene (for example mouse gene transfected into human cells is annotated to record for mouse gene).
- DO NOT annotate the genes, if they are named for cells and pathways.

## Disease

- Annotate the diseased-related phenotypes but not other (e.g., short ear in PMID:17345627).
- DO NOT annotate the high-level diseases (e.g., “genetic disorder”).
  Excludes:
  - Cis-acting disease (PMID:12442272)
  - genetic disorders (PMID:18046082)
  - familial disorder (PMID:20806042)
- Annotate “drug addiction” to “disease”.
- Annotate the symptoms to diseases.
- DO NOT annotate overdose.
- DO NOT annotate the mental status and phenotypes to diseases unless the term is exactly recorded in MEDIC. e.g., decline in sympathetic tone (PMID:19067809)
- DO NOT annotate references to biological processes such as “tumorigenesis” or “cancerogenesis”.
- Annotate minimum necessary text spans for a disease. For example, select “hypertension” instead of “sustained hypertension.”, unless the span covers the prefix or the suffix can exactly match a specific concept identifier (e.g., “chronic bronchitis” to D029481).

## Chemical

- Annotate the chemical abbreviation with the dose. For example “In addition, GABA content of mice hippocampus treated with GFC75 plus P400 showed an increase of 46.90% when compared with seized mice.”, 75 and 400 suffixes are the doses. In this case, we annotate GFC75 and P400 as chemical spans. (PMID:24911645).

- DO NOT annotate antibodies to chemicals. (PMID:17595233) (PMID:20648600)
- DO NOT annotate saline, placebo, water, and juice.
- DO NOT annotate residue, free radicals.
- DO NOT annotate staining chemical (e.g., hematoxylin in PMID:24442316)
- DO NOT annotate vaccines.

## Species

- DO NOT annotate beyond species rank (e.g., annotate homo sapiens but do not annotate mammalian which is a taxonomy class)

## Variant

- DO NOT annotate residue of the gene modification.

## Conflict cases among different concept types

iterations.discrepancy_insight:
- **Pattern Insight — “Generic variant-class terms mislabeled as specific SequenceVariant instances”**
  - **Pattern Name:** Variant *type* noun ≠ Variant *identifier*
  - **Confusion Trigger:** Standalone/common-noun mentions of variation—especially plural/indefinite forms like **“polymorphisms”**, **“single nucleotide polymorphisms”**, **“SNPs”**, and categorical labels like **“AA genotype”**—occurring near gene names (e.g., *“SNPs in SLC2A2”*). The proximity to genes + variant vocabulary cues the model to over-tag as **SequenceVariant** even when no specific variant is stated.
  - **Contrastive Evidence:** In the True Positives, SequenceVariant annotations appear only when the text contains a **concrete, referential variant designator** (e.g., **“rs5393”**, **“+3100 T/G”**, **“+8365 C/T”**) that uniquely identifies a particular variant. Those strings have “ID/coordinate + allele” structure, unlike the discrepancy terms which denote only a *class* of variants.
  - **Linguistic Rule (Proposed):** Tag **SequenceVariant** **only if** the mention includes an **instance-level identifier** (e.g., `rs\d+`, HGVS-like patterns such as `c\.\d+[ACGT]>[ACGT]`, protein changes like `p\.[A-Z][a-z]{2}\d+[A-Z][a-z]{2}`, or position+alleles like `\+\d+\s*[ACGT]/[ACGT]`). Otherwise, if the span is a **generic variant-class noun** (“polymorphism(s)”, “SNP(s)”, “mutation(s)”, “genotype”) **without** an attached unique identifier/coordinate/allele specification, label it **O** (even when it appears in “in/of + GENE” contexts).
iterations.moderation_principle: - **IF** a mention describes a **variant class/category** using a common noun phrase (often plural/indefinite) and **lacks an instance-level identifier**—i.e., no unique alphanumeric ID, coordinate/position+allele pattern, or HGVS-like nucleotide/protein change—**THEN** label it **O** (do **not** annotate as **SequenceVariant**), even when it appears in gene-proximal contexts (e.g., within “in/of + GeneOrGeneProduct” prepositional phrases); **THIS RULE DOES NOT APPLY** when the mention contains an explicit, uniquely referential variant designator (ID/coordinate/change), in which case it **should** be annotated as **SequenceVariant**.

# Concept types

To the better understanding, we grouped those highly relevant entities to six concepts types as shown below:
(1) Gene: it includes genes, proteins, mRNA and other gene products.
(2) Chemical: it contents chemical and drug.
(3) Disease : it contents diseases, symptoms, and some disease-related phenotypes.
(4) Variant : it contents the genomic/protein variants (including substitutions, deletions, insertions, and others).
(5) Species: it includes the species in the hierarchical taxonomy of organisms.
(6) CellLine: cell line.

# Guideline of the entities

## General rules

- Annotate all the spans of all the six concept types.
- The full text can be accessed to clarify the concept spans and identifiers.
- The abbreviation and its long form should be annotated separately if possible. prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) in the text, “prostaglandin E2” and “PGE2” should be both annotated to chemicals with the same identifier (D015232).
- Annotate both the full name and abbreviation in one entity, if the boundary of the entity covers both of them. For instance, annotate “Deoxyguanosine kinase (dGK) deficiency” entirely to a disease (PMID:19394258).
- Annotate the composite entity spans (e.g., “MMP-1, -2”) entirely.
- Annotate the concept spans with misspelling (“HLRRC” in PMID:18366737).

## Gene

- Annotate the gene families including paralogs/orthologs (e.g., bone morphogenetic protein(bmp)), but DO NOT annotate the functional based families (e.g., tumor suppressor gene, protein kinase).
- Following the previous rule, if at least one of the gene family members mentioned in the text, the identifiers of those members are assigned to the family name (e.g., in “Cytochrome P-450 genes (CYP1A1, CYP2A6, CYP2D6, and CYP2E1)”, Cytochrome P-450 genes should be assigned with NCBI Gene: 1543,1548,1565,1571). If no family member is in the text, the first gene reached in the gene family should be assigned (e.g., matrix metalloproteinases to NCBI Gene:4312(MMP1)).
- In experimental studies, annotate the gene identifier corresponding to the organism/species that is the source of the gene (for example mouse gene transfected into human cells is annotated to record for mouse gene).
- DO NOT annotate the genes, if they are named for cells and pathways.

## Disease

- Annotate the diseased-related phenotypes but not other (e.g., short ear in PMID:17345627).
- DO NOT annotate the high-level diseases (e.g., “genetic disorder”).
  Excludes:
  - Cis-acting disease (PMID:12442272)
  - genetic disorders (PMID:18046082)
  - familial disorder (PMID:20806042)
- Annotate “drug addiction” to “disease”.
- Annotate the symptoms to diseases.
- DO NOT annotate overdose.
- DO NOT annotate the mental status and phenotypes to diseases unless the term is exactly recorded in MEDIC. e.g., decline in sympathetic tone (PMID:19067809)
- DO NOT annotate references to biological processes such as “tumorigenesis” or “cancerogenesis”.
- Annotate minimum necessary text spans for a disease. For example, select “hypertension” instead of “sustained hypertension.”, unless the span covers the prefix or the suffix can exactly match a specific concept identifier (e.g., “chronic bronchitis” to D029481).

## Chemical

- Annotate the chemical abbreviation with the dose. For example “In addition, GABA content of mice hippocampus treated with GFC75 plus P400 showed an increase of 46.90% when compared with seized mice.”, 75 and 400 suffixes are the doses. In this case, we annotate GFC75 and P400 as chemical spans. (PMID:24911645).

- DO NOT annotate residue, free radicals.
- DO NOT annotate staining chemical (e.g., hematoxylin in PMID:24442316)

## Species

You are an expert AI Moderator.

**GOAL:**
Update the official Annotation Guidelines to incorporate new "Moderation Principles" discovered from error analysis.

**CURRENT GUIDELINES:**
# Concept types

To the better understanding, we grouped those highly relevant entities to six concepts types as shown below:
(1) Gene: it includes genes, proteins, mRNA and other gene products.
(2) Chemical: it contents chemical and drug.
(3) Disease : it contents diseases, symptoms, and some disease-related phenotypes.
(4) Variant : it contents the genomic/protein variants (including substitutions, deletions, insertions, and others).
(5) Species: it includes the species in the hierarchical taxonomy of organisms.
(6) CellLine: cell line.

# Guideline of the entities

## General rules

- Annotate all the spans of all the six concept types.
- The full text can be accessed to clarify the concept spans and identifiers.
- The abbreviation and its long form should be annotated separately if possible. prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) in the text, “prostaglandin E2” and “PGE2” should be both annotated to chemicals with the same identifier (D015232).
- Annotate both the full name and abbreviation in one entity, if the boundary of the entity covers both of them. For instance, annotate “Deoxyguanosine kinase (dGK) deficiency” entirely to a disease (PMID:19394258).
- Annotate the composite entity spans (e.g., “MMP-1, -2”) entirely.
- Annotate the concept spans with misspelling (“HLRRC” in PMID:18366737).

## Gene

- Annotate the gene families including paralogs/orthologs (e.g., bone morphogenetic protein(bmp)), but DO NOT annotate the functional based families (e.g., tumor suppressor gene, protein kinase).
- Following the previous rule, if at least one of the gene family members mentioned in the text, the identifiers of those members are assigned to the family name (e.g., in “Cytochrome P-450 genes (CYP1A1, CYP2A6, CYP2D6, and CYP2E1)”, Cytochrome P-450 genes should be assigned with NCBI Gene: 1543,1548,1565,1571). If no family member is in the text, the first gene reached in the gene family should be assigned (e.g., matrix metalloproteinases to NCBI Gene:4312(MMP1)).
- In experimental studies, annotate the gene identifier corresponding to the organism/species that is the source of the gene (for example mouse gene transfected into human cells is annotated to record for mouse gene).
- DO NOT annotate the genes, if they are named for cells and pathways.

## Disease

- Annotate the diseased-related phenotypes but not other (e.g., short ear in PMID:17345627).
- DO NOT annotate the high-level diseases (e.g., “genetic disorder”).
  Excludes:
  - Cis-acting disease (PMID:12442272)
  - genetic disorders (PMID:18046082)
  - familial disorder (PMID:20806042)
- Annotate “drug addiction” to “disease”.
- Annotate the symptoms to diseases.
- DO NOT annotate overdose.
- DO NOT annotate the mental status and phenotypes to diseases unless the term is exactly recorded in MEDIC. e.g., decline in sympathetic tone (PMID:19067809)
- DO NOT annotate references to biological processes such as “tumorigenesis” or “cancerogenesis”.
- Annotate minimum necessary text spans for a disease. For example, select “hypertension” instead of “sustained hypertension.”, unless the span covers the prefix or the suffix can exactly match a specific concept identifier (e.g., “chronic bronchitis” to D029481).

## Chemical

- Annotate the chemical abbreviation with the dose. For example “In addition, GABA content of mice hippocampus treated with GFC75 plus P400 showed an increase of 46.90% when compared with seized mice.”, 75 and 400 suffixes are the doses. In this case, we annotate GFC75 and P400 as chemical spans. (PMID:24911645).
- Annotate the chemical resource for extracts, e.g., “ethanolic extract of Daucus carota seeds (DCE)” in PMID:16755009; “grape seed proanthocyanidin extract” in PMID:11334364.
- DO NOT annotate antibodies to chemicals. (PMID:17595233) (PMID:20648600)
- DO NOT annotate saline, placebo, water, and juice.
- DO NOT annotate residue, free radicals.
- DO NOT annotate staining chemical (e.g., hematoxylin in PMID:24442316)
- DO NOT annotate vaccines.

## Species

- DO NOT annotate beyond species rank (e.g., annotate homo sapiens but do not annotate mammalian which is a taxonomy class)

## Variant

- Annotate SequenceVariant ONLY when the mention is an instance-level, uniquely referential variant designator, such as:
  - an rsID or similar database identifier (e.g., “rs5393”);
  - an explicit coordinate/position + allele/change pattern (e.g., “+3100 T/G”, “-308 G>A”);
  - an HGVS-like nucleotide/protein change (e.g., “c.76A>G”, “p.Val600Glu”, “IVS2+1G>T”);

  - We don’t annotate “coagulation inhibitors” in PMID:17003923

- Annotate spans with morphological variations such as adjectives. For instance, annotate “hypertensive” to “hypertension”, “psychiatric” to “Mental Disorders” and “VLCAD-deficient” to “VLCAD-deficiency”.

# Concept types

To the better understanding, we grouped those highly relevant entities to six concepts types as shown below:
(1) Gene: it includes genes, proteins, mRNA and other gene products.
(2) Chemical: it contents chemical and drug.
(3) Disease : it contents diseases, symptoms, and some disease-related phenotypes.
(4) Variant : it contents the genomic/protein variants (including substitutions, deletions, insertions, and others).
(5) Species: it includes the species in the hierarchical taxonomy of organisms. This also includes **implicit Homo sapiens** mentions when human study participants are referred to only by role/demographic labels (see **Species** section).
(6) CellLine: cell line.

# Guideline of the entities

## General rules

- Annotate all the spans of all the six concept types.
- The full text can be accessed to clarify the concept spans and identifiers.
- The abbreviation and its long form should be annotated separately if possible. prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) in the text, “prostaglandin E2” and “PGE2” should be both annotated to chemicals with the same identifier (D015232).
- Annotate both the full name and abbreviation in one entity, if the boundary of the entity covers both of them. For instance, annotate “Deoxyguanosine kinase (dGK) deficiency” entirely to a disease (PMID:19394258).
- Annotate the composite entity spans (e.g., “MMP-1, -2”) entirely.
- Annotate the concept spans with misspelling (“HLRRC” in PMID:18366737).
- When deciding whether a mention is a **Species** (OrganismTaxon), consider that **humans may be referenced implicitly** via participant role/demographic labels (e.g., “patients”, “controls”, “subjects”) in clinical/epidemiologic/genetic contexts; in such cases, annotate as **Homo sapiens** (see **Species** section for scope and exclusions).

## Gene

- Annotate the gene families including paralogs/orthologs (e.g., bone morphogenetic protein(bmp)), but DO NOT annotate the functional based families (e.g., tumor suppressor gene, protein kinase).
- Following the previous rule, if at least one of the gene family members mentioned in the text, the identifiers of those members are assigned to the family name (e.g., in “Cytochrome P-450 genes (CYP1A1, CYP2A6, CYP2D6, and CYP2E1)”, Cytochrome P-450 genes should be assigned with NCBI Gene: 1543,1548,1565,1571). If no family member is in the text, the first gene reached in the gene family should be assigned (e.g., matrix metalloproteinases to NCBI Gene:4312(MMP1)).
- In experimental studies, annotate the gene identifier corresponding to the organism/species that is the source of the gene (for example mouse gene transfected into human cells is annotated to record for mouse gene).
- DO NOT annotate the genes, if they are named for cells and pathways.

## Disease

- Annotate the diseased-related phenotypes but not other (e.g., short ear in PMID:17345627).
- DO NOT annotate the high-level diseases (e.g., “genetic disorder”).
  Excludes:
  - Cis-acting disease (PMID:12442272)
  - genetic disorders (PMID:18046082)
  - familial disorder (PMID:20806042)
- Annotate “drug addiction” to “disease”.
- Annotate the symptoms to diseases.
- DO NOT annotate overdose.
- DO NOT annotate the mental status and phenotypes to diseases unless the term is exactly recorded in MEDIC. e.g., decline in sympathetic tone (PMID:19067809)
- DO NOT annotate references to biological processes such as “tumorigenesis” or “cancerogenesis”.
- Annotate minimum necessary text spans for a disease. For example, select “hypertension” instead of “sustained hypertension.”, unless the span covers the prefix or the suffix can exactly match a specific concept identifier (e.g., “chronic bronchitis” to D029481).

## Chemical

- Annotate the chemical abbreviation with the dose. For example “In addition, GABA content of mice hippocampus treated with GFC75 plus P400 showed an increase of 46.90% when compared with seized mice.”, 75 and 400 suffixes are the doses. In this case, we annotate GFC75 and P400 as chemical spans. (PMID:24911645).
- Annotate the chemical resource for extracts, e.g., “ethanolic extract of Daucus carota seeds (DCE)” in PMID:16755009; “grape seed proanthocyanidin extract” in PMID:11334364.
- DO NOT annotate antibodies to chemicals. (PMID:17595233) (PMID:20648600)
- DO NOT annotate saline, placebo, water, and juice.
- DO NOT annotate residue, free radicals.
- DO NOT annotate staining chemical (e.g., hematoxylin in PMID:24442316)
- DO NOT annotate vaccines.

## Species

- Annotate explicit species mentions at the species rank (e.g., “human”, “Homo sapiens”, “rat(s)”, “mouse/mice”, “zebrafish”, “E. coli”, “HIV-1”).
- DO NOT annotate beyond species rank (e.g., annotate homo sapiens but do not annotate mammalian which is a taxonomy class).

- **Implicit human participants (new principle)**:
  - **IF** a noun phrase refers to **human clinical/research participants** only via **role/demographic labels** (common nouns denoting people in a study or case report), and the surrounding context contains **clinical/epidemiologic/genetic cues**, **THEN** annotate that span as `OrganismTaxon` (implicit *Homo sapiens*).
  - Typical **role/demographic labels** include (non-exhaustive): “patient(s)”, “case(s)”, “case patient(s)”, “control(s)”, “control subject(s)”, “subject(s)”, “participant(s)”, “carrier(s)”, “male(s)”, “female(s)”, “men”, “women”, “child(ren)”, “infant(s)”, “family/families” (when used to denote enrolled/assessed families in a genetic/clinical study), and age/sex-described subject NPs like “a 12-year-old female”.
  - Typical **qualifying cues** include (non-exhaustive): diagnosis/phenotypes/symptoms, treatment/medication, “case-control” framing, epidemiologic study design language, genotyping/sequencing/variant testing, odds ratios/CI/p-values tied to groups, and subject descriptors (age/sex, affected/carrier status) used as study variables.
  - **Boundary guidance**: annotate the minimal noun phrase that denotes the participant group/individual (e.g., annotate “patients”, “controls”, “subjects”; optionally include attached age/sex descriptors if they are part of the same noun phrase, e.g., “12-year-old female”).
  - **This does NOT apply** when:
    - the noun phrase denotes a **non-human participant/group**, or the participant species is explicitly non-human in the local context (e.g., “rats”, “mice”, “zebrafish”; in “control group of rats”, do **not** annotate “control group” as Homo sapiens);
    - the noun phrase refers to **non-participant humans** in general/discourse roles without subject-level clinical/genetic context (e.g., “authors”, “researchers”, “clinicians”, “surgeons”, “nurses”, “we”, “they” as investigators);
    - the mention is purely generic about people without being tied to a study/case context (no clinical/epidemiologic/genetic cues).

## Variant

- Annotate SequenceVariant ONLY when the mention is an instance-level, uniquely referential variant designator, such as:
  - an rsID or similar database identifier (e.g., “rs5393”);
  - an explicit coordinate/position + allele/change pattern (e.g., “+3100 T/G”, “-308 G>A”);
  - an HGVS-like nucleotide/protein change (e.g., “c.76A>G”, “p.Val600Glu”, “IVS2+1G>T”);
  - other explicit, uniquely identifying variant notations that clearly point to a specific variant instance.
- IF a mention describes a variant class/category using a common noun phrase (often plural/indefinite) and lacks an instance-level identifier (i.e., no unique alphanumeric ID, coordinate/position+allele pattern, or HGVS-like nucleotide/protein change), THEN label it O (do NOT annotate as SequenceVariant), even when it appears in gene-proximal contexts (e.g., within “in/of + GeneOrGeneProduct” prepositional phrases).
  - Examples to label O (unless accompanied by an explicit instance-level designator elsewhere in the same mention span): “mutations”, “polymorphisms”, “single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs)”, “sequence variants”, “genetic variation”, “variant allele(s)”, “risk variants”, “haplotypes” (when no explicit haplotype name/designator is given).
  - This rule DOES NOT APPLY when the mention itself contains an explicit, uniquely referential variant designator; in that case, annotate that explicit designator as SequenceVariant (e.g., annotate “rs5393”; annotate “+3100 T/G”).
- DO NOT annotate residue of the gene modification.

## Conflict cases among different concept types

- [Gene/Disease] If the disease and gene share the same name, e.g., adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD) gene, annotate the concept following the below cases:
  - Adrenoleukodystrophy gene > GeneOrGeneProduct
  - Adrenoleukodystrophy patient > DiseaseOrPhenotypicFeature
  - ALD gene > GeneOrGeneProduct
  - ALD patient > DiseaseOrPhenotypicFeature
  - adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD) gene > GeneOrGeneProduct
  - adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD) patient > DiseaseOrPhenotypicFeature
- Annotate the concept with longer spans. For instance, Deoxyguanosine kinase (dGK) deficiency (MESH:C580039) instead Deoxyguanosine kinase (in PMID:19394258).
- Annotate the prefix of the corresponding species to the gene span separately (e.g., “human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-DRB1” to “human” to species and “leukocyte antigen (HLA)-DRB1” to gene).
- Annotate the virus spans (e.g., HIV-1 and HBV) to species. But annotate the infection of the virus to disease (e.g., “HIV-1 infected” maps to MESH: D015658).
- Some of the proteins can be chemicals for particular usage or purpose. We annotate the organic compounds to proteins. While, we annotate the proteins or molecules as the biologic medical products to treat diseases .
- Annotate the alleles to variants rather than chemicals, DO NOT annotate the amino acids to chemicals.
- The rule for antagonist/agonist/blocker/inhibitor: If the sentence mentions a drug/chemical and then tells the target gene, we annotate both the chemical and the gene.
- Following the previous rule, we annotate the mention to a gene if the inhibitor/blockage/agonist is part of the gene name.
  - e.g., “plasminogen activator inhibitor-1” in PMID:16167916
- Following the previous rule, if “<gene> inhibitors/agonists” is mentioned in the context of a family of compounds, without mentioning a specific drug, We annotate the entire mention (“<gene> inhibitors/agonists”) as a chemical.
  - “Methadone dose, presence of cytochrome P-450 3A4 inhibitors” in PMID:16801510
- We don’t annotate functions of genes that are described as inhibitors or activators of processes.
  - We don’t annotate “coagulation inhibitors” in PMID:17003923

## Others

- Annotate spans with morphological variations such as adjectives. For instance, annotate “hypertensive” to “hypertension”, “psychiatric” to “Mental Disorders” and “VLCAD-deficient” to “VLCAD-deficiency”.
- The suffixes of the gene/protein (e.g., “kinase” of “dGK kinase”, “gene” of “ESR1 gene”) are ignored unless the meaning is changed without the suffix (e.g., “gene” in “Becker muscular dystrophy gene”).
- DO NOT annotate the general terms such as: disease, syndrome, deficiency, complications, gene, drug, protein, nucleotide, etc. However, the disease terms such as pain, cancer, tumor, and death should be retained.
